headline: Smart glasses maker Even Realities hits $1B valuation with $150M funding from Meituan, Tencent
summary: Shenzhen-based Even Realities secured $150M in funding, valuing the smart glasses startup at $1 billion. Their G2 glasses prioritize privacy with a camera-free, heads-up display.
details: Even Realities, a three-year-old startup, has achieved a $1 billion valuation after raising $150 million in a pre-Series B funding round. The investment was led by Meituan and existing backer Tencent.

Founded by ex-Apple engineers in 2023, Even Realities focuses on display-first smart glasses, contrasting rivals who emphasize camera-equipped devices for content capture and AI. CEO Will Wang states their approach prioritizes user privacy.

The company quickly launched its first product, the G1, in 2024, which Wang described as the lightest waveguide smart glasses on the market at the time. Even Realities surpassed its 10,000-unit sales target and grew from 30-40 staff in 2024 to 300-400 today.

Their latest flagship, the G2, released last November, entirely omits a camera. Instead, it features a heads-up display that feeds information to the wearer, controlled by a companion ring called the Even R1.

Wang emphasizes that removing the camera is a key part of their privacy philosophy, recognizing smart glasses as highly personal devices. Privacy is integrated into both hardware and software design, with features like real-time audio transcription (not recording) and encrypted user data, adhering to strict European privacy standards.
Even's power users leverage 'Conversate,' a copilot that reads conversations in real time, explaining jargon or suggesting follow-ups, then syncing a summary to their phone.

The company has heavily invested in optics, developing a proprietary technology called Even HAO (Holistic Adaptive Optics). This end-to-end design integrates the microchip, waveguide, and prescription support from the outset.

Over half of Even's users are in the U.S., its fastest-growing market, which also hosts the majority of its developer community. The company currently sells in the U.S., Japan, South Korea, the Middle East, and Europe, but not yet in China, despite manufacturing there.

Even's frames retail for $599 before tax, with prescription lenses or the companion ring adding $200-$300, bringing the average order to approximately $1,000. Wang notes that their customer base primarily consists of male professionals aged 30-50, with about a third being company executives.

headline_marked: [[AI agents enable 'vibe coding']] for faster dev, but require careful human oversight
headline: AI agents enable 'vibe coding' for faster dev, but require careful human oversight
summary: An engineer spent a weekend building a project almost entirely by talking to an AI agent, experiencing 'vibe coding'. The process dramatically speeds up development, allowing for rapid iteration, but requires constant human oversight to avoid shipping errors.
details: An engineer spent a weekend, about six hours, building a small project almost entirely by talking to an AI agent. This 'vibe coding' approach involved minimal typing and no tutorials, resulting in a working prototype by Sunday night.

Vibe coding means describing desired outcomes, with the AI agent writing, running, and debugging code autonomously. This shifts the developer's role from typing every line to steering the agent and reviewing its output.

The new process drastically cuts development time; a script that once took two hours now takes under ten minutes. This rapid feedback loop encourages experimentation, allowing developers to test multiple approaches quickly.

However, the AI's effectiveness is directly tied to the clarity of the human's prompts. Vague instructions yield vague code, while precise commands like 'Add a retry that backs off and stops after 30 seconds' produce exact results.

A significant risk is the AI being 'confidently wrong,' delivering professional-looking but incorrect code. Developers must diligently read and understand the generated code to catch potential bugs before deployment.

Rapid, numerous changes by the agent can also lead to the developer losing track of the project's evolution. It becomes crucial to pause and review modifications to maintain understanding and control over the codebase.

The core shift is from being a typist to a director, focusing on 'what to build and why' rather than 'how.' This mirrors working with CI pipelines or Terraform, where repetitive tasks are automated, and human judgment guides the overall strategy.

Ultimately, vibe coding is a powerful tool that, when used carefully, offloads tedious tasks and frees up energy for critical decisions. Used lazily, it can lead to shipping code that isn't fully understood, highlighting the need for responsible application.
